summary:
Catalunya stands under Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 1 March 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons. The statute applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, Catalunya included. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, by simple declaration with no requirement of a prior gender-dysphoria diagnosis or two years of medical treatment, and the law provides for corresponding adaptation of identity documents. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the statute regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. Its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Other operative provisions of the same statute include a ban on medically unnecessary normalising surgeries on intersex children before they can consent, expanded access to assisted reproduction, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and prohibitions on LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2 July 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation. Human Rights Watch reported on 16 February 2023 that the Congress of Deputies approved the law, placing the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition; the provision allowing recognition from age 12 proved contentious.

Access to sex-separated facilities in Spain rests on legal gender self-determination rather than biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Catalunya also operates its own statute, Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014, published in DOGC núm. 6730 on 17 October 2014, the autonomous LGTBI-rights law after which the 2010s wave of Spanish regional LGTBI laws followed. It defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms ensuring that administrative documentation reflects gender identity. Implementation of the state framework, including Ley 4/2023, falls to the Generalitat de Catalunya.
tangentialFactors:
With an administrative self-declaration regime, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change; that ranking is a dated baseline predating Ley 4/2023 and should not be read as a measurement of the current regime.

Catalunya has a record of moving ahead of the rest of Spain on relationship recognition. The Ley de Parejas of 30 June 1998 was the first Spanish couples law allowing homosexual couples minimum legal provisions, and the Generalitat de Catalunya's Ley 11/2014 prompted the 2010s wave of autonomous LGTBI laws across the autonomous communities.

The two enforcement decisions cited for the gender-identity aggravating circumstance, in Vigo and Valencia, were handed down outside Catalunya. They evidence how Spanish courts apply the aggravation nationally rather than how Catalan courts have applied it.
localsOnly:
Ley 11/2014 extends protections across education, health, employment and sport, and broadened the Observatorio Catalán del Deporte to act against violence and discrimination in sport. It also guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures such as body identification, burial and handling of personal effects.

The statute's sanctioning machinery is regional. Article 35 sanctions minor breaches by reference to the indicador de renda de suficiència de Catalunya, in amounts between seven days' and three months' worth of that indicator, and Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, with the Síndic de Greuges able to instigate proceedings.

Residents also operate under the older Spanish instruments that remain in force alongside Ley 4/2023: same-sex marriage since 2 July 2005 and the 2007 gender-identity law. Rectification applications already pending when Ley 4/2023 entered into force are handled under its transitory provisions rather than restarted.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents how the Generalitat de Catalunya has implemented the document-adaptation duty under Ley 4/2023 in practice, including processing times or which Catalan office handles applications. That remains unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory contains no reported decisions from Catalan courts applying the transfobia aggravating circumstance, and no Cataluña-specific data on violence against trans people. Whether the Vigo and Valencia pattern of enforcement holds in Catalunya is unresolved.

The claim that facility access follows the civil-registry gender marker rests on the parent framework's characterisation of Spanish practice; no Catalan or Spanish instrument text on single-sex spaces is quoted in this inventory, and no case law on the point is sourced.

The 2016 comparative survey predates Ley 4/2023 by seven years and does not measure the current legal position.
